name: Octocog alfa
route_note: IV injection on demand or as prophylaxis, typically every other day to three times weekly

discovery.by: Genentech (Jane Gitschier, William Wood and colleagues) and Genetics Institute (John Toole and colleagues)
discovery.note: The human factor VIII gene, one of the largest then known, was cloned and expressed in mammalian cells.

tagline: Full-length recombinant factor VIII replacing the clotting factor missing in haemophilia A
summary: Octocog alfa is full-length recombinant human coagulation factor VIII, produced in Chinese hamster ovary or baby hamster kidney cells. It replaces the deficient factor in haemophilia A for treatment and prevention of bleeding, removing the viral risks of plasma-derived concentrates.
mechanism: Factor VIII circulates bound to von Willebrand factor. When activated by thrombin, factor VIIIa acts as a cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic tenase complex on phospholipid surfaces, accelerating activation of factor X and hence thrombin generation.
Infused octocog alfa temporarily restores factor VIII activity in people with haemophilia A, allowing normal haemostasis. Its effect wanes over hours, requiring repeated dosing for prophylaxis.
uses: Treatment and control of bleeding in haemophilia A
Routine prophylaxis to reduce bleeding frequency

history.title: Gene cloned
history.detail: Two groups clone and express the human factor VIII gene.

history.title: Viral crisis
history.detail: Plasma-derived concentrates had transmitted HIV and hepatitis C to many people with haemophilia, creating demand for recombinant products.

history.title: Albumin-free
history.detail: Advate approved, made without added human or animal plasma proteins.

history.title: SIPPET
history.detail: A randomised trial finds higher inhibitor incidence with recombinant than plasma-derived factor VIII in previously untreated patients.

facts: Up to about 30% of previously untreated people with severe haemophilia A develop neutralising inhibitors against infused factor VIII.
